name: Psilothrum (ancient depilatory)

card.summary: Psilothrum was a Greek and Roman depilatory preparation used to remove body hair and leave smooth skin.
card.note: Ancient depilatories included caustic mineral ingredients; modern hair-removal products are different.

quick.overview:
Psilothrum (also spelled psilotrum, from the Greek psilothron) was an ointment or paste used in classical Greece and Rome to remove body hair. Smooth skin was an ideal of grooming for many Roman women and for men within limits, so depilatory preparations were part of the toilette.
Ancient sources name it alongside another depilatory, dropax. Surviving descriptions of ingredients are limited, but chemical depilatories of the period are generally associated with caustic mineral preparations, and Romans also used resin paste, shaving, plucking and pumice.
quick.how: Ancient users applied the paste to the skin and removed it with the hair; bathhouse attendants (alipili) and household slaves performed hair removal for bathers. Plucking, resin strips, scraping with pumice and shaving were used alongside it.
quick.risks: Caustic depilatory mixtures could irritate or burn skin, and arsenic-containing mixtures such as orpiment pastes are toxic. Modern readers should treat these as historical practices.

lead: Psilothrum (Latin psilothrum or psilotrum, from Greek ψίλωθρον) was a depilatory used in ancient Greece and Rome to take hair off the body, giving the smooth look then favoured in many grooming ideals.[1] It is listed together with a second depilatory, dropax.[1]

Hair removal in Rome followed social expectations: apart from head hair, body hair on women was widely seen as unattractive, and women removed it by shaving, plucking, stripping with resin paste or scraping with pumice. Men were expected to groom moderately, since removing too much hair was read as effeminate.[2] Specialist attendants called alipili removed hair for bathers.[1]

Historical reference works give little on psilothrum's exact recipe. Caustic pastes of slaked lime and arsenic trisulfide (orpiment) are documented as traditional depilatories elsewhere, and Greek sources name the mineral arsenikon, but a direct link to psilothrum is not established.[1]

angle.text: Psilothrum was used to take body hair off so the skin looked smooth, in line with classical grooming norms. It is the ancestor, in purpose, of modern chemical depilatory creams.

paras: Psilothrum is named in descriptions of ancient hair removal as a depilatory preparation, alongside dropax.[1] Precise formulas vary by source and are not settled.

sections.h: Context: hair removal in Greece and Rome
paras: Roman women removed body hair by shaving, plucking, resin-paste stripping or pumice, and depilation could be criticised in older women, who were seen as groomed mainly for sex.[2] Men's moderate depilation was acceptable; the emperor Elagabalus was said to have removed all his body hair, which upset Romans.[2] Plucking eyebrows to tidy them began in the 1st century BCE.[2] Suetonius reports that Augustus singed his leg hair with hot nutshells.[1]

A paste of slaked lime, water, wood ash and yellow orpiment (arsenic trisulfide), called vajibt, is still reported in rural India and Iran, and the Greek word for orpiment is noted in the literature.[1] Chemical depilatories for women were reportedly introduced in al-Andalus in the 9th century.[1]

timeline.event: Eyebrow plucking for tidiness begins in Rome.[2]
Psilothrum and dropax recorded as depilatories in Greece and Rome.[1]
